items.title: Unit 2: Ask Questions (driving question board): A tugboat pair guides a huge container ship into a harbor, one pulling from the front-left and one pushing from the right. What questions do you have about how several forces can combine to steer such a heavy object?

body.html: This is an open prompt, so there is no single correct answer. Good questions are testable and connect to forces, direction, and changes in motion. Work (sample questions, written here). Why does the ship not simply move in the direction of one tug's pull? How do you find the combined effect of two pushes that are not in the same direction? Does a bigger angle between the tow lines make the tugs less effective? What forces other than the tugs (water drag, wind) act on the ship? Is "force" a quantity that needs both a size and a direction, like displacement?

answer.html: Sample questions are listed above; every question should be about forces, direction, or how the ship's motion changes.

items.title: Module 5: Encounter the Phenomenon and CER: Crews spread sand on an icy road before cars drive on it. Make a claim about why, and explain your reasoning. (Data: tire on icy pavement has μₛ = 0.12 and μₖ = 0.08; tire on sand-covered ice has μₛ = 0.45 and μₖ = 0.35.)

answer.html: Sand increases the coefficient of friction between tires and ice, so the tires can supply enough friction to accelerate, stop, and steer safely.

items.title: Check Your Progress 12 (Lesson 1): Can the magnitude of a displacement ever be greater than the distance traveled? Explain, and give an example.

body.html: Distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement is the straight-line change in position, with direction (a vector). A straight line is the shortest path between two points.

Any path between the start and the end is at least as long as the straight line joining them. So the displacement magnitude is never more than the distance. They are equal only for straight-line motion without reversing. Example: jog around a 400 m track and return to the start. The distance is 400 m, but the displacement is 0. Another: walk 30 m east then 40 m north. The distance is 70 m, while the displacement is 50 m.

answer.html: No. The displacement magnitude is at most the distance traveled, and equals it only for straight-line motion in one direction.

items.title: Check Your Progress 13 (Lesson 1): (a) Show graphically that 𝑃+ 𝑄= 𝑄+ 𝑃, for 𝑃= 7.0 units along the +x axis and 𝑄= 4.0 units at 60° above +x. (b) For ordinary numbers, which of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and exponentiation (𝑎𝑏 ) are commutative? Give examples.

body.html: Draw 𝑃, then place the tail of 𝑄 at the tip of 𝑃; the resultant goes from the first tail to the final tip. Then draw 𝑄 first and place 𝑃's tail at its tip. Both paths are two sides of the same parallelogram and end at the same point, so the resultant is the same arrow. In components: 𝑅<sub>𝑥</sub>= 7.0 + 4.0 cos60° = 9.0 and 𝑅<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0 + 4.0 sin60° = 3.5, so 𝑅= 9.6 at 21° above the +𝑥 axis either way.

Work. Addition: 2 + 7 = 7 + 2 = 9, commutative. Multiplication: 2 × 7 = 7 × 2 = 14, commutative. Subtraction: 7 −2 = 5 but 2 −7 = −5, not commutative. Division: 8 / 2 = 4 but 2 / 8 = 0.25, not commutative. Exponentiation: 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 but 3<sup>2</sup> = 9, not commutative.

answer.html: Placing the vectors tip to tail in either order produces the same resultant (the diagonal of the parallelogram), 9.6 at 21°, so 𝑃+ 𝑄= 𝑄+ 𝑃.
(b) Addition and multiplication are commutative; subtraction, division, and exponentiation are not (examples above).

items.title: Check Your Progress 14 (Lesson 1, Critical Thinking): (a) Can three displacements of 2.0 m, 3.0 m, and 8.0 m add to zero? (b) Can three displacements of 4.0 m, 5.0 m, and 8.0 m add to zero? Explain.

body.html: The resultant is zero only if the vectors, placed tip to tail, close into a loop. Three vectors form a closed triangle only if the longest is no greater than the sum of the other two.

(a) 2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0 m, which is less than 8.0 m. The two short sides cannot reach across the long side, so no triangle closes. (b) 4.0 + 5.0 = 9.0 m, which is more than 8.0 m, so a triangle exists. By the law of cosines the interior angles are cos<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup> (<sup>4.0</sup><sup>2</sup><sup> + 8.0</sup><sup>2</sup><sup> −</sup><sup>5.0</sup><sup>2</sup>
) = 30.8° between the 4.0 m and 8.0 m sides, and 125.1° between the 4.0 m and 5.0 m sides (the third angle is 24.1°). Walking the three sides returns you to the start.

answer.html: (a) No. (b) Yes; the displacements form a closed triangle with sides 4.0 m, 5.0 m, and 8.0 m. Check. In (b) the longest side (8.0 m) is less than the sum of the others (9.0 m); in (a) it is not.

items.title: Module 5: Encounter the Phenomenon and CER, Why is a specialized train washing the train tracks?

question.html: Prompt: Make a claim about why the train is washing the tracks, and explain your reasoning.

body.html: A train moves and stops because of friction between steel wheels and steel rails. The traction force a wheel can get is at most 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup> (static friction), and the braking force is also limited by friction. Anything that lowers 𝜇 (wet leaf film, oil, dirt) lowers the maximum friction force. Work (sample CER written here).
The tracks are washed to remove contamination that lowers the friction between wheels and rails.

Friction force depends on the surfaces (the coefficient 𝜇) and the normal force (Table 2: steel on steel 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.78, but only 0.15 with castor oil). A thin slick layer cuts 𝜇 by a large factor.

The largest friction force available is 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>. With a lower 𝜇 the train cannot accelerate as fast (wheels spin) and cannot stop as quickly (wheels slide, so the stopping distance is longer). Washing the rails raises 𝜇 back to its normal value and keeps the train safe.

answer.html: The tracks are washed to remove slippery contaminants, which restores the coefficient of friction so the wheels can push and stop the train safely.

Three forces act: two rope tensions and gravity (free-body diagram). Add components. Gravity is 𝑚𝑔= (3.20)(9.80) = 31.4 N downward. The ground can only push up (a normal force), and it only does so when the box is pressed onto it.

𝐹<sub>𝑥</sub>= 20.4 cos120° + 17.7 cos55° = −10.20 + 10.15 = −0.05 N 𝐹<sub>𝑦</sub>= 20.4 sin120° + 17.7 sin55° −𝑚𝑔= 17.67 + 14.50 −31.36 = + 0.8 N The two ropes pull up with 32.2 N, which is more than the weight 31.4 N. So the box leaves the ground and the normal force is zero.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>net,</sub><sub> 𝑥</sub>≈−0.05 N (essentially zero) and 𝐹<sub>net,</sub><sub> 𝑦</sub>≈+ 0.8 N (upward) Check. The girls pull horizontally in nearly opposite directions with nearly equal pulls, so the box rises almost straight up, slowly, because the net force is tiny.

items.title: Check Your Progress 11 (Lesson 1), Vectors K, L, M (Figure 9)

question.html: From Figure 9: 𝐾 points left with magnitude 4.0 (its 𝑥-component is −4.0); 𝐿 points right with magnitude 6.0; 𝑀 has magnitude 5.0 at 37° above the horizontal.
(c) 𝐿−𝐾. Subtracting 𝐾 means adding −𝐾, which points right with magnitude 4.0.

body.html: Resolve each vector with 𝐴<sub>𝑥</sub>= 𝐴cos𝜃, 𝐴<sub>𝑦</sub>= 𝐴sin𝜃, then add components.

answer.html: (a) 𝐾= ( −4.0, 0), 𝐿= (6.0, 0), 𝑀= (4.0, 3.0) in the same (unspecified) units.
(b) 𝐾+ 𝐿+ 𝑀 has magnitude 6.7 at 27° above the +𝑥 axis (components 6.0 and 3.0).
(c) 𝐿−𝐾= 10.0 in the +𝑥 direction (0°). Check. 𝐾 and 𝐿 are opposite, so they mostly cancel in the sum and the sum is dominated by 𝑀; in (c) they reinforce.

items.title: Check Your Progress 12 (Lesson 1), Are distance and displacement always the same? Example.

body.html: Distance is the total path length (a scalar). Displacement is the straight-line change in position, with direction (a vector).

They match only for motion along a straight line without reversing. Example: walk 100 m north, then 100 m south. The distance is 200 m, but you end where you began, so the displacement is 0. A square lap of a 100 m block is another example.

answer.html: No. They are equal in magnitude only for straight-line motion in one direction; walking once around a block gives a nonzero distance but zero displacement.

items.title: Check Your Progress 13 (Lesson 1), Commutative operations (a) Show graphically that 𝑀+ 𝐿= 𝐿+ 𝑀.

question.html: (b) Are addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division commutative?

body.html: Draw 𝑀 then place the tail of 𝐿 at the tip of 𝑀; the resultant goes from the first tail to the final tip. Then draw 𝐿 first and place 𝑀's tail at its tip. Both paths are two sides of the same parallelogram and end at the same point, so the resultant is the same arrow. In components: 𝑅<sub>𝑥</sub>= 6.0 + 4.0 = 10.0 and 𝑅<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0 + 3.0 = 3.0, so 𝑅= 10.4 at 17° above the +𝑥 axis either way.

Work. Addition: 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 = 8, commutative. Multiplication: 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 = 15, commutative. Subtraction: 5 −3 = 2 but 3 −5 = −2, not commutative. Division: 6 / 3 = 2 but 3 / 6 = 0.5, not commutative.
(b) Examples.

answer.html: Placing the vectors tip to tail in either order produces the same resultant (the diagonal of the parallelogram), 10.4 at 17°, so 𝑀+ 𝐿= 𝐿+ 𝑀.
(b) Addition and multiplication are commutative; subtraction and division are not (examples above).

items.title: Check Your Progress 14 (Lesson 1, Critical Thinking), Can two unequal displacements sum to zero? Three?

body.html: The resultant is zero only if the vectors, placed tip to tail, close into a loop.

Two vectors can only close if they lie on the same line, are opposite, and have equal length. Unequal lengths leave a leftover. So two unequal displacements cannot sum to zero. Three vectors can form a closed triangle as long as the longest is less than the sum of the other two. For example 3 m, 4 m, 5 m arranged as a right triangle return you to the start.

answer.html: Two unequal displacements cannot give zero. Three unequal displacements can (e.g., 3 m, 4 m, 5 m tip to tail form a closed triangle). Check. The longest side (5 m) is less than the sum of the other two (7 m), so a closed triangle exists.
